sentences.text: The Four-Day Week Is Right for the Wrong Reasons
Supporters of the four-day week usually argue from happiness.
Workers sleep more, they report less stress, and they say they feel respected.
All of that is true.
However, happiness is a weak foundation for a policy that changes how a whole economy schedules itself, since a happy workforce is not automatically a productive one.
The stronger case rests on attention.
On the one hand, a five-day week gives every employee two empty days at the weekend, and many use them badly.
On the other hand, a four-day week forces a company to ask which meetings are worth holding.
In other words, the policy works because it removes waste, not because it grants a gift.
Consider what the trials show.
In one pilot, a software firm cut its weekly hours from forty to thirty-two.
Output stayed flat.
The firm did not become more efficient overnight; rather, it stopped doing the things nobody valued.
Meetings fell by a third, and the status reports that no one read were dropped.
Still, the firm kept every customer.
Critics make a fair objection.
Not every job has slack to cut.
A nurse cannot skip a shift, and a bus driver cannot drive the route faster.
That is, the gains are real only where the work can be compressed.
A hospital that adopts the policy without more staff simply moves the burden onto the remaining days.
Whether the policy helps depends on the job, and no slogan can settle it.
Some defenders reply that the critics ignore the evidence.
They are wrong to say so.
The best trials were run in offices, and offices are the easiest place to remove waste.
So the results say little about factories, shops, or clinics.
Meanwhile, the loudest advocates quote the office numbers as if they applied everywhere.
Either the policy is a general rule or it is a tool for particular firms.
It cannot be both.
If it is a rule, the law should require it, and the nurse and the bus driver will carry the cost.
If it is a tool, each firm should test it, and the law should stay out of the way.
I favor the second reading, because it matches what the evidence supports.
There is also a cost that few people discuss.
Then again, perhaps it is not a cost.
A shorter week pushes work into fewer hours, and fewer hours mean higher intensity.
Some employees thrive on this.
Others burn out faster, for the pressure of a compressed week is real.
Since the trials relied on volunteers, they probably attracted people who liked the idea.
None of this means the idea is bad.
Although the happiness argument is weak, the attention argument is strong, and it deserves a fair hearing.
A firm that tests a shorter week, measures its output honestly, and keeps the change only if the numbers hold has made a good decision.
Likewise, a firm that rejects the idea after a real test has also made a good decision.
In short, the four-day week is a useful experiment and a poor mandate.
Its supporters should stop selling joy and start publishing output data.
Its critics should stop treating one failed hospital pilot as proof against every office.
Both sides would learn more from a shared spreadsheet than from another slogan.
Overall, the sensible course is modest.
Let firms run honest trials, let them publish the results, and let the law wait for the evidence.
If the results are as strong as the supporters claim, nobody will need to be forced.

overview.gist: The text argues that the four-day week works best by cutting wasted time, not by making workers happier. It holds that the policy suits some jobs but not all, so firms should test it themselves rather than be forced to adopt it.
